title: Access Control and Conditional Access for AVD
summary: RBAC decides who can manage the AVD control plane; Conditional Access decides who even gets in. This lesson separates the two and shows how they interlock: the built-in Desktop Virtualization roles from Contributor down to User Session Operator, the data-plane Desktop Virtualization User role that actually grants app group access, and the Conditional Access cloud apps — Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows Cloud Login — that must both be targeted once single sign-on is enabled. You'll also cover MFA licensing, sign-in frequency behavior per app, the one app you must never add to an MFA policy, and the extra step Microsoft Entra joined session hosts need.
objectives: Map each built-in Desktop Virtualization RBAC role to the operational tier it serves, from full control-plane management to helpdesk session operations
Distinguish control-plane RBAC roles from the data-plane Desktop Virtualization User role that grants app group access
Configure a Conditional Access policy that correctly targets both the Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows Cloud Login cloud apps
Explain why the Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider app must be excluded from MFA-enforcing Conditional Access policies
Configure sign-in frequency per app and apply the extra Conditional Access step required for Microsoft Entra joined session hosts

quiz.q: Which built-in role lets a helpdesk operator send messages, disconnect, and log off user sessions without any host pool or session host management rights?
options: Desktop Virtualization User Session Operator
Desktop Virtualization Contributor
Desktop Virtualization Session Host Operator
Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor
quiz.why: User Session Operator allows sending messages, disconnecting sessions, and logging users off, but doesn't allow host pool or session host management such as removing hosts or changing drain mode.

quiz.q: A user is assigned Desktop Virtualization Contributor at the subscription scope but still can't assign users to an application group. What's missing?
options: They need Desktop Virtualization Reader in addition
They also need the User Access Administrator role
They need to be a Global Administrator
Nothing — Contributor should already allow this
quiz.why: Desktop Virtualization Contributor manages AVD resources but explicitly does not grant user or group assignment; that requires the User Access Administrator role (or equivalent) in addition.

quiz.q: Which Conditional Access cloud app enforces reauthentication for the session host sign-in specifically, when single sign-on is enabled?
options: Azure Virtual Desktop
Microsoft Remote Desktop
Windows Cloud Login
Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider
quiz.why: With SSO enabled, the Windows Cloud Login app governs the session host sign-in event and its own sign-in frequency; the Azure Virtual Desktop app governs subscription, feed refresh, and the gateway connection.

quiz.q: Which app should you deliberately exclude from an MFA-enforcing Conditional Access policy for AVD?
options: Windows Cloud Login
Azure Virtual Desktop
Microsoft Remote Desktop
Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider
quiz.why: The Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider app (app ID 50e95039-b200-4007-bc97-8d5790743a63) is used only to retrieve the user's resource feed and shouldn't have multifactor authentication applied, or feed discovery breaks.

quiz.q: A user has been granted the Desktop Virtualization User role, scoped to a single application group, with no other RBAC assignment. What can they do?
options: Use the applications or desktop published through that application group as a non-administrative user
Manage the host pool that backs the application group
View all AVD resources in the subscription
Assign other users to the application group
quiz.why: Desktop Virtualization User is a data-plane role granting only the useApplications action — it lets the assigned user consume the published resource, nothing administrative.

quiz.q: In three to four sentences, explain the difference between assigning a user the Desktop Virtualization User role on an application group and adding that user to the group targeted by a Conditional Access policy on the Azure Virtual Desktop app. What does each control decide?
quiz.answer: The Desktop Virtualization User role is an Azure RBAC data-plane assignment that decides authorization — whether a signed-in, already-authenticated user is allowed to use a specific application group's published desktop or apps. Conditional Access targeting the Azure Virtual Desktop app decides authentication — the conditions such as MFA, device compliance, location, and sign-in frequency a user must satisfy before Microsoft Entra ID issues them a token to reach the AVD service at all. A user can pass Conditional Access and still be denied by RBAC if they're not assigned to the app group, and conversely can be correctly RBAC-assigned but blocked entirely if they fail the Conditional Access policy.
quiz.why: RBAC (Desktop Virtualization User) governs authorization to specific AVD resources; Conditional Access governs the authentication conditions required to reach the service and session host at all. They are complementary, independent layers that both must pass.

body_markdown:
## Two Different Questions, Two Different Systems

"Can this admin manage the host pool?" and "can this user even reach AVD right now?" are answered by two completely separate systems. Azure role-based access control (RBAC) answers the first: it's authorization for the control plane and, in one special case, the data plane. Microsoft Entra Conditional Access answers the second: it's authentication policy, evaluated on every sign-in, regardless of what RBAC role someone holds. Confusing the two is the single most common AVD access-control mistake — teams lock down RBAC tightly and leave Conditional Access wide open, or vice versa, and wonder why access still isn't behaving as expected.

## The Desktop Virtualization Role Family

AVD doesn't have its own Owner role — you use the standard Azure Owner role for that — but it ships a deliberately granular set of built-in roles so you can separate host pool management from application group management from session operations:

| Role | Scope of control | Typical assignee |
|---|---|---|
| **Desktop Virtualization Contributor** | Manage all AVD resources except user/group assignment | Platform team |
| **Desktop Virtualization Reader** | View all AVD resources, no changes | Auditors, read-only ops |
| **Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor** | Manage all aspects of a host pool | Host pool owners |
| **Desktop Virtualization Application Group Contributor** | Manage an application group, except user/group assignment | App owners |
| **Desktop Virtualization Workspace Contributor** | Manage workspaces | Platform team |
| **Desktop Virtualization Session Host Operator** | View and remove session hosts, change drain mode | Operations engineers |
| **Desktop Virtualization User Session Operator** | Message, disconnect, and log off user sessions only | Helpdesk / Tier 1-2 |
| **Desktop Virtualization Virtual Machine Contributor** | Create, delete, start, stop VMs for the AVD resource provider | Automation identities |
| **Desktop Virtualization User** | Data-plane: use published apps/desktop | End users |

Notice the deliberate gap: Contributor roles manage resources but never grant user or group assignment. If you want an admin to both build a host pool and assign users to its app groups, you pair the relevant Contributor role with **User Access Administrator**. This separation exists so that platform engineers who provision infrastructure don't automatically also control who gets access to it — a genuine least-privilege boundary, not an accident.

For day-to-day operations, the two roles you'll assign most after initial build-out are **Desktop Virtualization Session Host Operator** (drain mode, host removal — your operations rotation) and **Desktop Virtualization User Session Operator** (message, disconnect, log off — your helpdesk tier, deliberately unable to touch host pool configuration).

## Data Plane vs Control Plane: The User Role Is Different

Every role above except one is a **control-plane** role — it grants permissions over the AVD resource objects themselves (host pools, application groups, workspaces) via Azure Resource Manager `actions`. **Desktop Virtualization User** is different: it's a **data-plane** role, granting only the `Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization/applicationGroups/useApplications/action` `dataAction`. This is the role — scoped to an application group — that actually determines which end users can see and launch a given desktop or RemoteApp. Assigning end users this role (directly or, more commonly, through a group) at the application group scope is how you populate a workspace's feed for them. Get the scope wrong — assign at the wrong application group, or forget the assignment for a new app group — and users authenticate fine but see nothing to connect to.

## Conditional Access: Which Apps Actually Govern AVD

Every AVD connection can, in principle, be authenticated to twice: once to the AVD **service** (subscribing to your feed, connecting to the gateway) and once to the **session host** (signing in to Windows), if single sign-on is enabled. Each phase is a different Microsoft Entra app in Conditional Access, so a policy targeting only one leaves the other phase unprotected:

- **Azure Virtual Desktop** (app ID `9cdead84-a844-4324-93f2-b2e6bb768d07`) — applies when a user subscribes, authenticates to the gateway during a connection, and when diagnostics are sent. This app was previously named *Windows Virtual Desktop*; if your resource provider was registered before the rename, you may still see the old name with the same app ID.
- **Windows Cloud Login** (app ID `270efc09-cd0d-444b-a71f-39af4910ec45`) — applies when the user authenticates to the session host, but only when SSO is enabled. Microsoft recommends matching your Conditional Access policy between this app and the Azure Virtual Desktop app, **except for sign-in frequency**, which behaves differently on each (see below).

If you enable SSO and only target the Azure Virtual Desktop app with your MFA policy, the session host sign-in phase goes unprotected — a real gap, not a theoretical one.

## The App You Must Never Put Behind MFA

There's a third app you'll encounter while searching the Conditional Access app picker: **Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider** (app ID `50e95039-b200-4007-bc97-8d5790743a63`). This app is used purely to retrieve the user's resource feed — it isn't a user-facing sign-in event — and Microsoft explicitly states it shouldn't have multifactor authentication applied. Adding it to an MFA-enforcing policy blocks feed discovery for your users. Know this app by name specifically so you don't select it by mistake when searching for "Azure Virtual" in the app picker.

## Sign-In Frequency: Two Apps, Two Behaviors

Sign-in frequency policies control how often a user must reauthenticate, and the two AVD apps behave differently under the same setting:

- On the **Azure Virtual Desktop** app, reauthentication is enforced when the user subscribes, manually refreshes their feed, or authenticates to the gateway. After the period expires, background feed refresh and diagnostics silently fail until the user's next interactive sign-in — there's no hard block, just a quiet feed staleness.
- On the **Windows Cloud Login** app, reauthentication is enforced when the user signs in to a session host with SSO enabled — and this is the only app where the **Every time** option is supported, prompting reauthentication roughly every 5 to 10 minutes after the last authentication, for scenarios that need very tight session control.

## Entra-Joined Session Hosts: The Extra Step

For Microsoft Entra joined session hosts specifically, there's a documented gotcha: for connections to succeed, you must either disable the legacy per-user MFA sign-in method, or — if you want to keep strong methods like Windows Hello for Business intact without loosening that — exclude the **Azure Windows VM Sign-In** app from your Conditional Access policy. Skipping this step is a common cause of "MFA works everywhere except my Entra-joined AVD hosts" tickets.

## Putting It Together: A Layered Access Design

A solid AVD access design layers, rather than merges, these controls: RBAC Contributor and Session Host/User Session Operator roles for admins and helpdesk at the control plane; Desktop Virtualization User assignments per application group for end users at the data plane; and a Conditional Access policy pair — one on Azure Virtual Desktop, one on Windows Cloud Login, both requiring MFA and a sensible sign-in frequency, deliberately excluding the ARM Provider app — governing authentication for everyone, regardless of their RBAC role. Lesson 3 builds on this by hardening the session hosts themselves once a user is actually connected.

slides.sub: RBAC decides who manages it; Conditional Access decides who gets in
slides.narration: In this lesson we separate two systems that get confused constantly: Azure role-based access control, which governs who can manage Azure Virtual Desktop resources, and Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, which governs who is even allowed to authenticate. We'll walk the built-in Desktop Virtualization roles, the special data-plane role that actually grants app access, the Conditional Access apps that target AVD, and the one app you should never put behind multifactor authentication.

slides.title: Two Different Questions
bullets: RBAC: can this admin manage the host pool or application group?
Conditional Access: can this user authenticate right now, under these conditions?
They are independent systems, evaluated separately
Locking down only one leaves the other wide open
slides.narration: Every access problem in Azure Virtual Desktop reduces to two separate questions. Role-based access control asks whether an admin can manage a resource. Conditional Access asks whether a user is allowed to authenticate at all, right now, under the conditions Microsoft Entra ID observes. These are independent systems. Locking one down tightly while leaving the other open is the most common access control mistake teams make.

slides.title: The Desktop Virtualization Role Family
bullets: Contributor manages everything except user or group assignment
Host Pool, Application Group, and Workspace Contributor roles split management further
Session Host Operator: drain mode and host removal, for operations
User Session Operator: message, disconnect, log off — for helpdesk only
slides.narration: Azure Virtual Desktop ships a deliberately granular set of built-in roles. Desktop Virtualization Contributor manages nearly everything but never grants user or group assignment on its own. Host Pool, Application Group, and Workspace Contributor roles split that management even further by resource type. For daily operations, Session Host Operator handles drain mode and host removal, while User Session Operator is scoped down to messaging, disconnecting, and logging off sessions, exactly what a helpdesk tier needs and nothing more.

slides.title: Contributor Doesn't Grant Assignment
bullets: Desktop Virtualization Contributor never grants user or group assignment
Assigning users requires User Access Administrator in addition
This is a deliberate least-privilege boundary, not an oversight
Platform engineers who build infrastructure don't automatically control access to it
slides.narration: Here's a gap that surprises new administrators. Desktop Virtualization Contributor lets you manage host pools, application groups, and workspaces, but it never lets you assign users or groups to them. To do that you also need the User Access Administrator role. This is a deliberate least-privilege boundary: the team that builds the infrastructure isn't automatically the team that decides who gets access to it.

slides.title: The Data-Plane Exception: Desktop Virtualization User
bullets: Every other role is control-plane: it manages the AVD resource objects
Desktop Virtualization User is data-plane: it grants useApplications only
Scoped to an application group, this determines what appears in a user's feed
Wrong scope means users authenticate fine but see nothing to connect to
slides.narration: Nearly every role we've covered is a control-plane role, managing the resource objects themselves. Desktop Virtualization User is different. It's a data-plane role granting only the useApplications permission, scoped to a specific application group. This is the assignment that actually determines what shows up in an end user's feed. Get the scope wrong, and users pass authentication perfectly but see nothing to connect to.

slides.title: Conditional Access: Two Apps, Two Phases
bullets: Azure Virtual Desktop app: subscription, feed refresh, gateway connection
Windows Cloud Login app: session host sign-in, only when SSO is enabled
A policy on only one app leaves the other authentication phase unprotected
Recommended: match policies between both apps, except sign-in frequency
slides.narration: Every AVD connection can authenticate twice: once to the service, and once to the session host if single sign-on is enabled. The Azure Virtual Desktop app governs the first phase, subscription, feed refresh, and the gateway connection. The Windows Cloud Login app governs the second phase, the session host sign-in itself. A Conditional Access policy that only targets the Azure Virtual Desktop app leaves that second phase completely unprotected once SSO is turned on.

slides.title: The App You Must Never Put Behind MFA
bullets: Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider app exists too
It's used only to retrieve the user's resource feed
It is explicitly not meant to require multifactor authentication
Adding it to an MFA policy silently breaks feed discovery
slides.narration: There's a third app in the picker that trips people up: the Azure Virtual Desktop Azure Resource Manager Provider app. It exists purely to retrieve a user's resource feed in the background, and Microsoft is explicit that it should never require multifactor authentication. If you accidentally include it in an MFA-enforcing policy, feed discovery breaks for your users, often with no obvious error pointing back to the cause.

slides.title: Sign-In Frequency Behaves Differently Per App
bullets: Azure Virtual Desktop app: silent feed/diagnostics failure after the period expires
Windows Cloud Login app: enforced at session host sign-in
Only Windows Cloud Login supports the Every time option
Every time reprompts roughly every 5 to 10 minutes after last auth
slides.narration: Sign-in frequency doesn't behave identically across the two apps. On the Azure Virtual Desktop app, once the period expires, feed refresh and diagnostics just quietly fail in the background until the user's next interactive sign-in. On the Windows Cloud Login app, reauthentication is enforced right at the session host sign-in, and it's the only app that supports the Every time option, which reprompts users roughly every five to ten minutes after their last authentication for very tight control.

slides.title: The Entra-Joined Session Host Gotcha
bullets: Microsoft Entra joined session hosts need an extra Conditional Access step
Disable the legacy per-user MFA sign-in method, or
Exclude the Azure Windows VM Sign-In app from your policy
Skipping this is a common cause of MFA failing only on Entra-joined hosts
slides.narration: There's one more documented gotcha specific to Microsoft Entra joined session hosts. For connections to succeed, you either need to disable the legacy per-user multifactor authentication sign-in method, or, if you want to preserve strong methods like Windows Hello for Business, exclude the Azure Windows VM Sign-In app from your Conditional Access policy. Missing this step is a frequent cause of tickets where MFA works everywhere except on Entra-joined AVD hosts specifically.

slides.title: A Layered Access Design
bullets: RBAC: Contributor and Operator roles for admins and helpdesk
Data plane: Desktop Virtualization User per application group for end users
Conditional Access: matched policies on both AVD apps, ARM Provider excluded
Next: harden the session host itself once a user is connected
slides.narration: A solid access design layers all of this rather than merging it. Role-based access control handles admins and helpdesk at the control plane. Desktop Virtualization User assignments, scoped per application group, handle what end users can actually see and use. And a matched pair of Conditional Access policies, on both AVD apps, with the ARM Provider app deliberately excluded, governs authentication for everyone regardless of role. Lesson 3 picks up from here and hardens the session host itself, once a user is actually connected to it.
